Structure matters as much as values - same values in a different shape is false.
Short-circuit evaluation means unequal values stop the recursion early.

complexity.why: each pair of nodes is compared once, stopping early on any mismatch.

followups.q: Symmetric tree.
followups.a: The same parallel recursion, but compare left against right and right against left - a mirror rather than an identity.

followups.q: Subtree of another tree.
followups.a: Run this check at every node of the larger tree. O(n*m) naively; serialise both and use KMP for O(n+m).

learnings.insight: A tree is symmetric when its left subtree mirrors its right. The recursion therefore takes two nodes and compares left-against-right crosswise - which is Same Tree with one pair of arguments swapped.
learnings.trick: `mirror(a,b)` returns `a->val == b->val && mirror(a->left, b->right) && mirror(a->right, b->left)`. The crossing in the two recursive calls is the whole difference.
edge_cases: Compare a->left with b->right, NOT b->left. Getting this wrong tests identity instead of symmetry.
Both null is true; one null is false.
A single node is symmetric.

complexity.why: each pair of mirrored nodes is compared once.

followups.q: Do it iteratively.
followups.a: A queue holding pairs of nodes, enqueued in mirrored order. The pairing is what preserves the crossing.

followups.q: How does this relate to Invert Binary Tree?
followups.a: A tree is symmetric exactly when it equals its own inversion. You could invert and compare, though that mutates or copies unnecessarily.

learnings.insight: Swap every node's children. Three lines, and famous only because of the story about its author failing an interview on it. The value here is that it is the simplest possible structural mutation.
learnings.trick: Swap left and right, then recurse into both. Order does not matter - recurse first or swap first, both work, because the swap is local.
edge_cases: Null returns null.
The tree is mutated in place; return the root.
An iterative BFS version is equally short.

complexity.why: every node is visited once and performs a constant-time swap.

followups.q: Does it matter whether you swap before or after recursing?
followups.a: No. The swap only affects the node's own two pointers, and the recursive calls operate on whole subtrees regardless of which side they now hang from.

followups.q: Iterative version.
followups.a: BFS with a queue, swapping each dequeued node's children before enqueuing them.

learnings.insight: Computing height at every node and checking balance separately is O(n^2). The bottom-up fix is to return the height AND signal imbalance in the same value - conventionally -1 for 'already unbalanced below here'.
learnings.trick: Return -1 to propagate failure. Any child returning -1 short-circuits immediately, so the whole check is a single traversal.
edge_cases: -1 must propagate upward without further computation.
Balance is defined per node, not globally - every node's subtrees must differ by at most 1.
Null returns 0.

complexity.why: one traversal computing heights, versus O(n^2) for recomputing height at every node. The sentinel is what fuses the two questions into one pass.

followups.q: Why is the naive version O(n^2)?
followups.a: Height at the root costs O(n), and it is recomputed at every node. On a degenerate tree that is n calls of O(n) work.

followups.q: Return the height instead of a boolean.
followups.a: That is the point of the sentinel - one return value answers both questions, which is the general trick for fusing two tree traversals.

learnings.insight: The diameter through a node is leftHeight + rightHeight, but the value returned to the parent is 1 + max(leftHeight, rightHeight). Confusing those two is the single most common bug in tree problems, and this is where you learn the distinction.
learnings.trick: Update a global best with l + r inside the recursion, but return 1 + max(l, r). The answer through a node uses BOTH children; the value that can extend upward uses only one.
edge_cases: The diameter counts EDGES, so it is l + r rather than l + r + 1.
The longest path need not pass through the root.
A single node has diameter 0.

complexity.why: one traversal, with each node contributing a constant-time update. Computing height separately at each node is O(n^2).

followups.q: Why can't you just return the diameter?
followups.a: The diameter through a node uses both subtrees and therefore cannot be extended by the parent. The parent needs a one-sided value. Two different quantities, one traversal.

followups.q: Maximum path sum instead of length.
followups.a: LC 124 - same skeleton, but clamp negative child contributions at zero, since excluding a negative subtree is always allowed.

learnings.insight: Carry the path down rather than reconstructing it on the way up. Passing the accumulated string by value is simple but copies at every node; passing a vector by reference with an explicit pop is the pattern that scales to harder path problems.
learnings.trick: Push the node, recurse, pop. Emit only at a leaf - a node with both children null, not merely a null node, or you emit each path twice.
edge_cases: A leaf is a node with BOTH children null. Recursing into nulls and emitting there duplicates every path.
Null root returns empty.
The pop after recursion is the backtrack; omitting it corrupts sibling paths.

complexity.why: n nodes, each path costing O(h) to format. The path vector is bounded by the height.

followups.q: Why check for a leaf rather than recursing into null?
followups.a: A node with one child would otherwise emit a path ending at the null side, producing duplicates and paths that do not end at a leaf.

followups.q: Sum root-to-leaf numbers.
followups.a: LC 129 - carry an integer built as `cur * 10 + val` instead of a string. Same skeleton, cheaper accumulation.

learnings.insight: Subtract as you descend rather than accumulating and comparing at the leaf. It reads more cleanly and the leaf test becomes 'does the remainder equal this node's value'.
learnings.trick: At a leaf, return `target == r->val`. Recurse with `target - r->val` into both children and OR the results.
edge_cases: Negative values mean you cannot prune on the remainder going negative.
The path must END at a leaf - a partial path summing correctly does not count.
Null root returns false even when the target is 0.

complexity.why: each node is visited at most once, with early exit on the first matching path.

followups.q: Return all such paths.
followups.a: LC 113 - carry the path vector and push a copy at every successful leaf. Backtrack with a pop after each recursive call.

followups.q: Paths that need not start at the root or end at a leaf.
followups.a: LC 437 - prefix sums in a hash map along the current root-to-node path, which is the tree version of Subarray Sum Equals K.

learnings.insight: Run Same Tree at every node of the larger tree. The naive bound is O(n*m), and the follow-up - serialise both with null sentinels and run KMP - is what makes this worth doing rather than a duplicate of Same Tree.
learnings.trick: At each node, if values match, try a full Same Tree comparison; otherwise recurse into both children. An early value check avoids most of the expensive comparisons.
edge_cases: An empty subRoot is trivially a subtree.
The match must be complete - a partial structural match does not count.
Serialisation must include null sentinels, or [1,2] and [1,null,2] serialise identically.

complexity.why: each of n nodes may trigger an O(m) comparison. Serialising both trees turns it into substring search, which KMP does in linear time.

followups.q: Make it O(n + m).
followups.a: Serialise both trees in preorder with null sentinels and delimiters, then run KMP. The sentinels are what make the serialisation injective.

followups.q: Why are delimiters needed as well as sentinels?
followups.a: Without them, values 1 and 12 are indistinguishable from 1,2 in the flattened string.

learnings.insight: Parallel recursion again, but constructive rather than comparative. When one side is null, the whole opposing subtree is the answer - returning it wholesale rather than copying node by node is both simpler and faster.
learnings.trick: `if (!a) return b; if (!b) return a;` then build a new node with the sum and recurse. Two lines handle every null case.
edge_cases: Returning the existing subtree shares nodes between input and output - fine here, but worth stating if mutation matters.
Both null returns null, which the first check handles.
Values may be negative; the sum is unconditional.

complexity.why: recursion stops as soon as either tree runs out, so only the overlapping region is traversed.

followups.q: Merge in place into the first tree.
followups.a: Assign into a->left and a->right rather than allocating. Saves memory but destroys the input, which the caller may not expect.

followups.q: Why is it O(min(n,m)) and not O(n+m)?
followups.a: Once one tree is exhausted the other is returned whole without traversal.

learnings.insight: A node cannot tell whether it is a left child - that information lives with the parent. Carrying an `isLeft` flag down the recursion is the general fix whenever a node needs context it does not own.
learnings.trick: Pass a boolean saying whether the current node is a left child. Add its value only when the flag is set AND it is a leaf.
edge_cases: A left child that is not a leaf contributes nothing, but must still be recursed into.
A single root node is not a left leaf.
Checking for a leaf from the parent works too - test `r->left && !r->left->left && !r->left->right`.

complexity.why: one traversal with a constant-time test per node.

followups.q: Do it without the flag.
followups.a: Test from the parent: if the left child exists and has no children, add it. Avoids the parameter but duplicates the leaf test.

followups.q: When else must context flow downward?
followups.a: Anywhere a node's answer depends on its ancestors - BST validation ranges, path prefix sums, and depth-aware problems.

problems.title: Average of Levels in Binary Tree

learnings.insight: A direct application of the level-order template with an aggregate per level instead of a list. The only real trap is overflow: a level of 10^4 nodes each at INT_MAX exceeds int comfortably.
learnings.trick: Accumulate the level sum in a long long or double, then divide by the captured level size.
edge_cases: Sum the level in long long - values reach INT_MAX and levels can be wide.
Divide by the size captured before the loop, not q.size() after it.
Null root returns empty.

complexity.why: one BFS with constant work per node.

followups.q: Why is overflow a real risk here?
followups.a: 10^4 nodes at 2^31-1 each sums past 2^45. Accumulating in int silently wraps and the average is nonsense.

learnings.insight: Collect each tree's leaves in left-to-right order and compare the sequences. The interesting version generates both sequences lazily and compares as it goes, which avoids materialising either.
learnings.trick: A DFS appending only at leaves gives the sequence in order. Compare the two vectors directly.
edge_cases: Order matters - the same leaf values in a different arrangement is false.
Different leaf counts fail immediately.
A single-node tree has one leaf: itself.

complexity.why: one traversal per tree, with the leaf sequences bounded by the node counts.

followups.q: Compare without storing either sequence.
followups.a: Run two iterative traversals in lockstep, advancing each to its next leaf and comparing. O(h) space instead of O(n), and it can exit early on the first mismatch.

learnings.insight: Compare each node against the root rather than against its parent. Both work here, but the root comparison makes the transitivity explicit and generalises to 'all nodes satisfy property P'.
learnings.trick: Pass the root's value down and check equality at every node. Short-circuit on the first mismatch.
edge_cases: A single node is univalued.
Null returns true, which makes the recursion terminate cleanly.
Checking against the parent works too, by transitivity.

complexity.why: one traversal with early exit.

followups.q: Longest univalue path.
followups.a: LC 687 - the bottom-up pattern again, extending only through children with the same value. A genuine step up from this.

learnings.insight: Another instance of returning one thing and accumulating another: the function returns the subtree sum while a global collects the tilt. Recognising this shape for the third time is the point of the repetition.
learnings.trick: Return the subtree sum. Add `abs(leftSum - rightSum)` to a running total inside the recursion.
edge_cases: Tilt is accumulated over ALL nodes, not just the root.
Sums can be negative; the tilt uses absolute difference.
Null returns 0 for both the sum and the tilt contribution.

complexity.why: one traversal. Computing each subtree sum independently would be O(n^2).

followups.q: Name the pattern.
followups.a: Return-one-value-accumulate-another. Diameter, maximum path sum, tilt, longest univalue path and distribute coins are all this.

followups.q: Distribute coins in a binary tree.
followups.a: LC 979 - return the excess coins, accumulate the absolute movement. Structurally identical, and the hardest instance of the pattern in this phase.

learnings.insight: Two facts are needed per node - its depth and its parent - and neither is available locally. Carrying both down the recursion, or capturing them during BFS, is the general answer to 'compare two nodes' relationship'.
learnings.trick: BFS is cleaner here: process level by level, and within a level check whether both targets appear and whether they share a parent. Same level plus different parents is the definition.
edge_cases: Same depth is not sufficient - siblings share a parent and are not cousins.
The root has no cousins.
Both values are guaranteed to exist and be distinct.

complexity.why: one traversal capturing depth and parent for both targets.

followups.q: Why check parents rather than just depth?
followups.a: Siblings are at the same depth but are explicitly excluded by the definition. The parent check is what distinguishes cousins from siblings.

followups.q: All nodes at distance k from a target.
followups.a: LC 863 - build parent pointers, then BFS outward treating the tree as an undirected graph. The same 'give nodes access to their parents' idea, scaled up.

learnings.insight: The binary case generalises by replacing 'max of two children' with 'max over a vector of children'. Nothing else changes, which is the point - the recursion never depended on there being exactly two.
learnings.trick: Loop over the children vector taking the maximum, then add one. An empty children vector makes a leaf return 1 naturally.
edge_cases: Null root returns 0.
A node with no children returns 1, handled by the loop not executing.
Children are stored in a vector, so null children do not appear.

complexity.why: every node and every edge is visited once.

followups.q: Diameter of an N-ary tree.
followups.a: Take the two LARGEST child depths rather than both children. The bottom-up pattern generalises the same way.

learnings.insight: Preorder on an N-ary tree is identical in structure. Iteratively, children must be pushed in REVERSE order, for exactly the same reason the binary version pushes right before left.
learnings.trick: Emit the node, then recurse over children in order. Iteratively, push children in reverse so the leftmost is popped first.
edge_cases: Reverse the push order in the iterative version.
Empty children vector is a leaf.
Null root returns empty.

complexity.why: each node is emitted once and each edge traversed once.

followups.q: Why reverse the push order?
followups.a: A stack emits in reverse insertion order, so pushing children left to right would visit them right to left.

learnings.insight: The reverse-a-modified-preorder trick generalises: emit the node, push children in FORWARD order, then reverse the whole result. Same shortcut as the binary case.
learnings.trick: Iteratively: emit node, push children left to right, then reverse the output at the end.
edge_cases: Push order is the opposite of the preorder version.
The final reversal is required.
Recursion is trivially a loop over children followed by an emit.

complexity.why: one traversal plus one reversal.

followups.q: Why does the reversal trick work for both binary and N-ary?
followups.a: It relies only on postorder being the reverse of a preorder with children visited in reverse - which is true for any branching factor.

learnings.insight: The level-order template with an inner loop over the children vector instead of two explicit pushes. The size snapshot still does all the work.
learnings.trick: Same `int sz = q.size()` snapshot, then enqueue every child of each dequeued node.
edge_cases: Enqueue all children, not just the first two.
Null root returns empty.
Children vectors contain no nulls.

complexity.why: every node is enqueued and dequeued once.

followups.q: How much of the binary template survives?
followups.a: All of it. Only the child enumeration changes, which is why learning the template once pays across both shapes.

learnings.insight: The right side view is the last node of each level. Once you see that, the entire problem is the level-order template with one line changed - which is why learning that template properly pays off repeatedly.
learnings.trick: BFS, and append the node when `i == sz - 1`. The DFS alternative visits right before left and records the first node seen at each new depth.
edge_cases: It is not 'all rightmost children' - a deep left subtree is visible when the right side is shorter.
Null root returns empty.
The DFS version must visit right first, or it records the left side.

complexity.why: one BFS with constant work per node.

followups.q: Left side view.
followups.a: Append when i == 0, or DFS visiting left before right. One character of difference.

followups.q: Why not just follow right pointers?
followups.a: A node's right child may be null while a deeper left descendant is still the rightmost visible node at its level.

learnings.insight: Traverse level by level enqueuing RIGHT before LEFT, and the last node dequeued is automatically the bottom-left. Inverting the enqueue order removes all the bookkeeping.
learnings.trick: BFS pushing right then left; whatever is dequeued last is the answer. No level tracking needed at all.
edge_cases: 'Bottom-left' means leftmost node of the DEEPEST level, not the leftmost leaf.
A single node is its own answer.
The DFS version must track maximum depth and only record on a strictly greater depth.

complexity.why: one BFS with no per-level structure, because the reversed enqueue order encodes the answer.

followups.q: DFS version.
followups.a: Track the maximum depth seen and record the value only when the current depth strictly exceeds it, visiting left first. Strict inequality is what keeps the leftmost.

followups.q: Why does reversing the enqueue order work?
followups.a: The last node dequeued is on the deepest level, and pushing right first means the leftmost of that level is dequeued last.

problems.title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree

learnings.insight: A node's status depends on its ancestors, not its descendants, so this is a TOP-DOWN problem rather than the usual bottom-up one. Carry the running maximum downward.
learnings.trick: Pass the maximum value seen on the path so far. Count the node if its value is at least that maximum, then recurse with the updated maximum.
edge_cases: The root is always good - initialise the running maximum to INT_MIN or the root's value.
Equal values count as good, so use >=, not >.
Values may be negative.

complexity.why: one traversal carrying a scalar. No information flows upward at all.

followups.q: Top-down versus bottom-up - how do you tell?
followups.a: Ask whether the node's answer depends on its ancestors or its descendants. Ancestors means pass state down; descendants means return values up.

followups.q: Which other problems are top-down?
followups.a: BST validation with ranges, path sums, and anything phrased 'on the path from the root'.

learnings.insight: Build the number as you descend with `cur * 10 + val` rather than collecting digits and assembling at the leaf. It is cheaper and it makes the leaf case a single return.
learnings.trick: Pass the accumulated value down. At a leaf return it; otherwise return the sum of both recursive calls. Nulls return 0 so they contribute nothing.
edge_cases: Only complete root-to-leaf paths count.
Null children return 0, which is why a one-child node does not double-count.
Depth is bounded, so the accumulated value fits in int per the constraints.

complexity.why: one traversal with constant work per node.

followups.q: Binary digits instead of decimal.
followups.a: LC 1022 - `cur * 2 + val`. The accumulation pattern is base-independent.

followups.q: Smallest string starting from leaf.
followups.a: LC 988 - build the string in reverse and compare lexicographically at each leaf. Harder, because string comparison is not a simple accumulation.

learnings.insight: Paths need not start at the root, so this is Subarray Sum Equals K on the root-to-node path. A hash map of prefix sums along the current path answers each node in O(1), and the map must be UNWOUND on the way back up.
learnings.trick: Maintain a map from prefix sum to count, seeded with {0: 1}. At each node add `map[cur - target]` to the answer, then recurse, then DECREMENT the map entry before returning.
edge_cases: Failing to decrement on the way back up counts paths from other branches.
Seed the map with {0, 1} for paths starting at the root.
Sums overflow int - use long long for the running prefix.
Negative values are permitted, which is why no pruning is possible.

complexity.why: each node does constant-time map work, and the map holds at most h entries because it is unwound. The naive all-pairs version is O(n^2).

followups.q: Why must the map be decremented?
followups.a: The map represents prefixes along the CURRENT path only. Leaving a sibling branch's entries in place counts paths that do not exist.

followups.q: Recognise the parent problem.
followups.a: It is Subarray Sum Equals K with the array replaced by a root-to-node path. Recognising that equivalence is worth more than the code.

problems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree

learnings.insight: Return the node itself if it matches either target, then let the recursion combine: if both sides return non-null, this node is the split point and therefore the LCA. Four lines, and the correctness argument is worth more than the code.
learnings.trick: `if (!r || r == p || r == q) return r;` then recurse both sides. Both non-null means return r; otherwise return whichever is non-null.
edge_cases: A node may be its own ancestor - if p is an ancestor of q, p is the LCA.
This assumes both nodes exist. If that is not guaranteed, a verification pass is needed.
Comparison is by pointer identity here, not by value.

complexity.why: one traversal with early return. Every node is visited at most once.

followups.q: What if a node might not exist?
followups.a: The bare algorithm returns the other node, which is wrong. Add a verification pass, or count found targets during the recursion.

followups.q: The BST version.
followups.a: LC 235 - far simpler. Descend while both targets are on the same side; the first node that splits them is the LCA. O(h) with no recursion.

followups.q: Many queries on the same tree.
followups.a: Binary lifting for O(log n) per query after O(n log n) preprocessing, or Euler tour plus sparse table for O(1) queries.

problems.title: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List

tuf.striver_title: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List

learnings.insight: Flattening in preorder order looks like it needs the successor of each node, which is awkward forward. Traversing in REVERSE preorder - right, left, node - means the previously visited node is always exactly the successor you need.
learnings.trick: Traverse right, then left, then the node. Keep a `prev` pointer; set `r->right = prev`, `r->left = nullptr`, then `prev = r`.
edge_cases: Left must be nulled, or the result is not a proper list.
prev starts as nullptr so the last node in preorder terminates the list.
The Morris-style O(1) version rewires using the left subtree's rightmost node.

complexity.why: one traversal rewiring two pointers per node. The O(1)-space version threads instead of recursing.

followups.q: Do it in O(1) space.
followups.a: For each node with a left child, find that subtree's rightmost node, attach the current right subtree there, move left to right, and null the left. Move on. This is Morris threading applied to flattening.

followups.q: Why reverse preorder?
followups.a: Forward preorder would overwrite the right pointer before its subtree was processed. Reversing means everything to the right is already flattened when you arrive.

problems.title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal

tuf.striver_title: Construct a BT from Preorder and Inorder

learnings.insight: Preorder gives you the root; inorder tells you how many nodes are on each side of it. Together they pin the tree down uniquely, and a hash map from value to inorder index is what keeps the construction linear.
learnings.trick: Consume preorder left to right with a shared index. For each call, take the root, look up its inorder position in O(1), and recurse LEFT before RIGHT - the preorder index must advance in that order.
edge_cases: Left must be built before right, because preorder is consumed sequentially.
Without the hash map, searching inorder is O(n) per node, giving O(n^2).
This assumes distinct values, which the constraints guarantee.

complexity.why: each node is constructed once with an O(1) index lookup. The map is the only extra space beyond the recursion.

followups.q: The postorder variant.
followups.a: Consume postorder from the END and build RIGHT before LEFT - postorder reversed is node-right-left.

followups.q: Can preorder plus postorder work?
followups.a: Not for a general binary tree - it cannot distinguish a single left child from a single right child. It does work for full binary trees.

followups.q: What if values repeat?
followups.a: The index map becomes ambiguous and the reconstruction is no longer unique. The constraint on distinctness is load-bearing.

problems.title: Construct Binary Tree from Inorder and Postorder Traversal

tuf.striver_title: Construct the Binary Tree from Postorder and Inorder Traversal

learnings.insight: The mirror of the preorder version. Postorder's LAST element is the root, so consume it from the end and build the RIGHT subtree before the left - because postorder reversed is node, right, left.
learnings.trick: Index into postorder from the back, decrementing. Recurse right first, then left. Same inorder hash map.
edge_cases: Right before left, or the postorder index desynchronises.
Consume from the end, not the front.
Same distinct-values assumption as the preorder variant.

complexity.why: one construction pass with O(1) index lookups.

followups.q: Why right before left?
followups.a: Reading postorder backwards gives node, right subtree, left subtree. Building in that order keeps the shared index aligned.

problems.title: Populating Next Right Pointers in Each Node

learnings.insight: BFS solves it in O(w) space. The follow-up demands O(1), and the perfect-tree guarantee is what makes it possible: every node has both children, so the next pointers of the level above form a ready-made linked list to walk.
learnings.trick: Use the current level's next pointers to traverse it while wiring the level below. `node->left->next = node->right` and `node->right->next = node->next->left`.
edge_cases: `node->next->left` requires a null check on node->next at the end of each level.
The perfect-tree guarantee is what makes both children always present.
The recursion-based version is O(h) stack, not O(1).

complexity.why: each node is visited once and wires two pointers. The already-built level above serves as the traversal structure, which is what removes the queue.

followups.q: The tree is no longer perfect.
followups.a: LC 117 - children may be missing, so you must scan forward along the next chain to find the next available child. A dummy head per level makes it manageable.

followups.q: Why is recursion not O(1) space?
followups.a: The call stack is O(h). Only the iterative level-walk achieves genuine constant space.

problems.title: Populating Next Right Pointers in Each Node II

learnings.insight: Without the perfect-tree guarantee, a node's next sibling may be several nodes along the level. A dummy head for the level being built turns that search into a simple append, which is the trick that makes the O(1) version tractable.
learnings.trick: Keep a dummy node and a tail pointer for the next level. Walk the current level via next pointers, appending each existing child to the tail. The next level's head is dummy.next.
edge_cases: The dummy must be reset at the start of every level.
Children may be absent on either side - append only non-null ones.
The last node of each level must end with a null next.

complexity.why: each node is appended exactly once and the walk uses pointers already built.

followups.q: Why does the dummy head help so much?
followups.a: It removes the 'is this the first node of the level' special case, exactly as a dummy head does in linked list problems. Same trick, different structure.

followups.q: Does this solution also work for LC 116?
followups.a: Yes - it is strictly more general. Writing this one first means you only learn one algorithm.

tuf.striver_title: Count total nodes in a complete BT

learnings.insight: Counting every node is O(n) and ignores the completeness guarantee. Exploiting it gives O(log^2 n): compare the leftmost and rightmost depths, and if they match the subtree is perfect, so its size is 2^h - 1 with no traversal at all.
learnings.trick: Walk left and right from each node measuring depths. Equal depths means a perfect subtree - return the formula. Otherwise recurse into both children.
edge_cases: Only one of the two recursive branches ever does real work, which is why it is log^2 and not linear.
Depth measurement is O(log n) and happens O(log n) times.
Use 1 << h, and watch for overflow at large heights.

complexity.why: at each of log n levels, one subtree is perfect and answered in O(1) after an O(log n) depth check. Only the other is recursed into.

followups.q: Why is only one branch ever recursed into?
followups.a: In a complete tree, at any node either the left subtree is perfect or the right one is. The perfect side is answered by formula, so recursion continues down a single path.

followups.q: Where else does 'exploit the structural guarantee' apply?
followups.a: Heaps, which are complete by definition - which is why they can live in an array with no pointers.

learnings.insight: The hardest instance of the return-one-accumulate-another pattern. The answer through a node uses both children; the value returned upward can use only one. Clamping negative contributions at zero is what handles negative values correctly.
learnings.trick: `l = max(0, dfs(left)); r = max(0, dfs(right)); best = max(best, val + l + r); return val + max(l, r);`. Four lines, and every one of them matters.
edge_cases: Clamping at 0 means a negative subtree is excluded rather than forced into the path.
The path need not touch the root and need not reach a leaf.
An all-negative tree returns the largest single value, which the clamp handles.
Initialise best to INT_MIN, not 0.

complexity.why: one traversal with constant work per node.

followups.q: Why clamp at zero?
followups.a: Including a negatively-summing subtree can only reduce the total, and the path is allowed to stop before it. max(0, ...) encodes that choice without a branch.

followups.q: Return the path itself.
followups.a: Record the node achieving each best, plus which children contributed, then reconstruct by walking down from the recorded node.

learnings.insight: Preorder alone cannot rebuild a tree, but preorder WITH null sentinels can - the sentinels encode exactly the shape information that ordering alone lacks. That is the whole design decision.
learnings.trick: Serialise preorder, emitting a marker such as '#' for every null, with a delimiter between tokens. Deserialise by consuming tokens in the same order, returning null on the marker.
edge_cases: Delimiters are needed as well as sentinels, or 1 and 12 are ambiguous against 1,2.
Negative values must survive the round trip.
Deserialisation consumes tokens in exactly the serialisation order - an index or stream shared across recursive calls.

complexity.why: each node produces one token and consumes one. The string is proportional to the node count.

followups.q: Why are sentinels enough when a second traversal was needed before?
followups.a: The nulls mark exactly where subtrees end, which is the structural information inorder was supplying. One annotated traversal replaces two plain ones.

followups.q: Serialise a BST more compactly.
followups.a: Preorder alone suffices, because the BST invariant supplies the shape. No sentinels needed - LC 449.

followups.q: Make it robust to duplicate values.
followups.a: It already is - unlike reconstruction from two traversals, the sentinel form never needs to look values up.

problems.title: All Nodes Distance K in Binary Tree

tuf.striver_title: Print all nodes at a distance of K in BT

learnings.insight: Distance in a tree runs in three directions - down both children and UP to the parent - but tree nodes have no parent pointer. Building a parent map converts the tree into an undirected graph, and then it is plain BFS.
learnings.trick: One DFS to record every node's parent in a hash map, then BFS outward from the target for exactly k levels, using a visited set so you do not walk back.
edge_cases: A visited set is mandatory - without it BFS oscillates between a node and its parent.
k = 0 returns the target itself.
k larger than the tree's reach returns empty.

complexity.why: one DFS to build the parent map and one BFS bounded by k levels, each visiting every node at most once.

followups.q: Why not solve it purely recursively?
followups.a: You can - compute the distance from the target to each node via the LCA - but the parent-map plus BFS is shorter, and the reframing is the transferable idea.

followups.q: Recognise the reframing.
followups.a: 'A tree is a graph with no cycles.' The moment a problem needs upward movement, add parent edges and reach for BFS or DFS on a graph.

learnings.insight: Tree DP with two states per node: the best total if this node is robbed, and the best if it is not. Returning a pair rather than a single number is what removes the exponential recomputation.
learnings.trick: Return {robbed, notRobbed}. robbed = val + left.notRobbed + right.notRobbed. notRobbed = max of each child's two options, summed.
edge_cases: notRobbed takes the MAX of each child's states, not the notRobbed one - you may still choose not to rob a child.
Null returns {0, 0}.
Values are non-negative here, so no clamping is needed.

complexity.why: one traversal returning a pair. Memoising a single-value recursion also works but is more machinery for the same result.

followups.q: Why return a pair instead of memoising?
followups.a: The pair makes the state explicit and needs no map. Memoising hides the same two states behind a cache keyed on (node, robbed).

followups.q: Name the general pattern.
followups.a: Tree DP: each node returns a small tuple of states, and the parent combines them. Binary Tree Cameras is the same idea with three states.

learnings.insight: Width counts the null gaps between the outermost nodes, so you must track positions rather than counts. Indexing nodes as in a heap - children at 2i and 2i+1 - gives the positions for free.
learnings.trick: BFS carrying (node, index). Width per level is lastIndex - firstIndex + 1. Normalise indices by subtracting the level's first index, or they overflow.
edge_cases: Indices overflow at depth ~60 without normalisation - subtract the level's first index from every node in it.
Use unsigned long long or normalise; a degenerate right-leaning tree hits this fast.
Nulls are not enqueued, but their positions are still implied by the index arithmetic.

complexity.why: one BFS with constant work per node. The index arithmetic is what accounts for gaps without enqueuing nulls.

followups.q: Why does normalisation prevent overflow?
followups.a: Indices double each level, so depth 60 exceeds 2^60. Subtracting the level's first index keeps every value small while preserving differences.

followups.q: Where else does heap indexing appear?
followups.a: Binary heaps themselves, and segment trees - any complete structure stored in a flat array.

learnings.insight: Diameter with a condition attached. A child only contributes if its value matches the current node's, which turns one comparison into the difference between this problem and LC 543.
learnings.trick: Compute each child's arm length, but zero it unless the child's value equals the node's. Update the best with the sum of both arms; return the larger arm plus one.
edge_cases: The value check happens AFTER recursing, since you need the child's arm length regardless.
The answer counts edges, so a single node gives 0.
Null returns 0.

complexity.why: one traversal with constant work per node.

followups.q: How does it differ from Diameter?
followups.a: Only in the conditional zeroing of each arm. Recognising a problem as 'X with a predicate' is faster than solving it fresh.

followups.q: Why recurse before checking the value?
followups.a: The recursion must still run to update the global best inside that subtree. Skipping it would miss answers entirely within the child.

learnings.insight: Return the EXCESS coins a subtree has - positive if surplus, negative if deficit - and accumulate the absolute value of what crosses each edge. The signed return value is what makes the accounting work.
learnings.trick: `excess = node->val - 1 + leftExcess + rightExcess`. Add `abs(leftExcess) + abs(rightExcess)` to the answer, since that is how many coins must physically cross those two edges.
edge_cases: Excess may be negative, meaning coins must flow INTO the subtree.
The -1 accounts for the node keeping one coin for itself.
The total number of coins equals the number of nodes, guaranteed.

complexity.why: one traversal. Each edge's traffic is counted exactly once, and the total is the sum over edges.

followups.q: Why is summing |excess| per edge correct?
followups.a: Each edge must carry exactly the net imbalance of the subtree below it. Moves along different edges are independent, so the total is their sum.

followups.q: Why can excess be negative and that still be fine?
followups.a: Direction does not affect the count of moves. The absolute value is what is being summed.

learnings.insight: Greedy from the leaves upward: never place a camera on a leaf, because its parent covers strictly more. Three states per node - needs cover, has camera, is covered - encode the decision, and the bottom-up order is what makes the greedy exact.
learnings.trick: Return one of three states. If either child needs cover, place a camera here. If either child has a camera, this node is covered. Otherwise it needs cover.
edge_cases: The root may end in the needs-cover state and require one final camera.
Null must return 'covered', or every leaf's parent is forced to place a camera.
Leaves must never hold cameras - the state machine enforces this implicitly.

complexity.why: one traversal with a constant-size state. The DP over all placements would be exponential.

followups.q: Why must null return 'covered'?
followups.a: Returning 'needs cover' would force a camera at every leaf, which is exactly the suboptimal placement the greedy avoids.

followups.q: Prove the leaf rule.
followups.a: Any camera on a leaf covers the leaf and its parent. Moving it to the parent covers the leaf, the parent, the parent's other child and the grandparent - strictly more, never less.

problems.title: Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree

learnings.insight: Assign each node a (column, row) coordinate, then group by column. The tie-breaking rule is the whole difficulty: same column and same row means order by VALUE, not by traversal order.
learnings.trick: DFS collecting (col, row, val) triples, then sort by col, then row, then value, and group. A map<int, map<int, multiset<int>>> does the grouping and sorting in one structure.
edge_cases: Ties at the same coordinate sort by value - this is the difference from LC 314.
Columns can be negative, so a map or an offset is needed.
Rows must be tracked as well as columns, since ordering within a column is top-down.

complexity.why: the sort dominates. Collection is linear; ordering the triples is the cost.

followups.q: How does it differ from the simpler vertical traversal?
followups.a: LC 314 uses traversal order for ties. This one requires value order, which forces an explicit sort rather than a BFS that happens to arrive in order.

followups.q: BFS instead of DFS.
followups.a: BFS gives rows in order automatically, so only the value tie-break needs sorting. Slightly less work overall.

problems.title: Check Completeness of a Binary Tree

learnings.insight: Enqueue nulls as well as real nodes. In a complete tree every null appears after every real node, so the check is simply: once a null has been seen, no real node may follow.
learnings.trick: BFS pushing both children unconditionally, including nulls. Set a flag on the first null dequeued; if any non-null appears afterwards, return false.
edge_cases: Nulls MUST be enqueued - this is the opposite of every other BFS here.
A single node is complete.
The queue can hold up to n nulls, which is fine at these constraints.

complexity.why: one BFS visiting every node and every null child once.

followups.q: Why does enqueuing nulls work?
followups.a: Completeness means all gaps are at the end of the last level. In level order that is exactly 'all nulls come after all nodes'.

followups.q: Index-based alternative.
followups.a: Assign heap indices and check that the maximum index equals the node count. Equivalent, and it connects to why heaps are stored in arrays.

learnings.insight: The naive construction finds the maximum in each range, which is O(n^2) on sorted input. The O(n) solution is a monotonic decreasing stack - the same structure as Next Greater Element, used constructively rather than analytically.
learnings.trick: Maintain a decreasing stack of nodes. The popped node becomes the new node's LEFT child; the new node becomes the last-popped survivor's RIGHT child.
edge_cases: Sorted input is exactly the O(n^2) worst case for the naive version.
Values are distinct by constraint, so there are no ties to resolve.
The final stack bottom is the root.

complexity.time: O(n) with the stack, O(n²) naive
complexity.why: each node is pushed and popped once. The recursive range version recomputes maxima repeatedly.

followups.q: Why does a monotonic stack build the right tree?
followups.a: The stack always holds the right spine of the tree built so far, in decreasing order. A new larger value displaces exactly the part of that spine it should become the parent of.

followups.q: Recognise the connection.
followups.a: This tree is the Cartesian tree of the array, and monotonic stacks are the standard way to build one in linear time.

learnings.insight: Prune bottom-up. A node can only be judged after its children have been pruned, because removing them may make it removable in turn - which is precisely what postorder ordering guarantees.
learnings.trick: Recurse into both children first, assigning the results back. Then return nullptr if the node is 0 and both children are now null.
edge_cases: Assign the recursive results back into left and right, or the pruning is discarded.
The cascade matters - pruning a child can make the parent prunable.
The root itself may be pruned away, returning null.

complexity.why: one postorder traversal. Repeated top-down passes until stable would be O(n·h).

followups.q: Why must this be postorder?
followups.a: A node's removability depends on its children AFTER they have been pruned. Preorder would judge it against the un-pruned subtree and miss cascading removals.

followups.q: Trim a BST to a value range.
followups.a: LC 669 - same bottom-up rewiring, but the BST invariant lets you skip whole subtrees instead of examining every node.

learnings.insight: The sum of the last level. With BFS you simply overwrite a running sum at each level and keep whatever survives - no depth tracking needed at all.
learnings.trick: BFS, computing each level's sum and assigning (not adding) it to the answer. The final assignment is the deepest level.
edge_cases: Assign rather than accumulate across levels.
A single node is its own deepest level.
The DFS version must reset the sum when a strictly greater depth is found.

complexity.why: one BFS with constant work per node.

followups.q: DFS version.
followups.a: Track the maximum depth; on a strictly greater depth reset the sum, on an equal depth add to it. The reset is what people forget.

learnings.insight: The string is read leaf-to-root, so build it in reverse as you descend and compare at each leaf. Lexicographic comparison is not an accumulation, which is why this is harder than Sum Root to Leaf Numbers.
learnings.trick: Prepend each character as you descend - or append and reverse at the leaf. Compare the completed string against the best so far with plain string comparison.
edge_cases: Shorter strings are not automatically smaller - 'ab' < 'aba' but 'b' > 'aba'.
Only complete root-to-leaf paths count.
Prepending is O(length) per node; appending and reversing once per leaf is cheaper.

complexity.why: each of up to n leaves builds and compares a string of length up to h.

followups.q: Why can't you prune early on a prefix comparison?
followups.a: A longer path may still be lexicographically smaller if it continues with smaller characters. Only complete strings are comparable.

followups.q: Why is this harder than summing root-to-leaf numbers?
followups.a: Addition is associative and can be accumulated downward. Lexicographic order depends on the whole string, so nothing can be finalised until the leaf.

learnings.insight: A node becomes a new root exactly when it survives and its parent did not. Passing that one boolean down, combined with bottom-up deletion, handles the whole problem.
learnings.trick: Recurse with an `isRoot` flag. If the node is deleted, its surviving children become roots. Use a hash set for the delete list so membership is O(1).
edge_cases: The original root is a root unless it is itself deleted.
Collect new roots during the traversal, not afterwards.
Children must be reassigned from the recursive calls, or deletions are lost.

complexity.why: one traversal with O(1) set lookups. The delete set is the only extra space beyond recursion.

followups.q: Why combine top-down and bottom-up here?
followups.a: The isRoot flag flows down; the rewiring flows up. Several tree problems need both directions, and separating them keeps the code honest.

followups.q: Why a set rather than scanning the delete list?
followups.a: Scanning would be O(k) per node for O(n·k) total. The set makes each check constant.

problems.title: Time Needed to Inform All Employees

learnings.insight: A general tree given as a parent array. Build children lists and the answer is the maximum root-to-leaf weighted depth - which is a DFS, not a BFS, because you want the longest path rather than the shortest.
learnings.trick: Invert the manager array into a children adjacency list, then DFS accumulating informTime and taking the maximum over all leaves.
edge_cases: The head has manager -1 and must be found, not assumed to be index 0.
Leaves have informTime 0 but that must not be assumed.
Recursion can be 10^5 deep - an explicit stack or BFS may be required.

complexity.why: building the adjacency list is linear, and the DFS visits every node once.

followups.q: Why maximum and not sum?
followups.a: Subordinates are informed in parallel, so the total time is set by the slowest chain, not the accumulated work.

followups.q: Recursion depth risk.
followups.a: A chain of 10^5 employees overflows the stack. Convert to an iterative DFS or a BFS carrying accumulated time.

tuf.striver_title: Check if a tree is a BST or not

learnings.insight: Comparing each node only against its parent is the classic wrong answer. A node deep in a left subtree must be smaller than EVERY ancestor above it, and only a propagated range carries that constraint.
learnings.trick: Pass (lo, hi) down, narrowing at each step. Use `long` bounds, or a tree containing INT_MIN breaks the sentinels. The inorder-strictly-increasing check is an equally valid alternative with no sentinels at all.
edge_cases: Root 10, left child 5, that node's right child 12 - passes a parent check, fails validation. This is the canonical counterexample.
Duplicates are not allowed, so comparisons are strict.
INT_MIN or INT_MAX values break int-typed sentinels - use long.

complexity.why: one traversal carrying two scalars. Every node is checked against its full ancestor constraint rather than just its parent.

followups.q: Give the counterexample for parent-only checking.
followups.a: [10, 5, 15, null, null, 6, 20]. The node 6 sits in the root's right subtree and is smaller than 10, yet passes every parent comparison.

followups.q: The inorder alternative.
followups.a: Traverse inorder and verify each value strictly exceeds the previous. No sentinels needed, and it extends naturally to Recover BST.

problems.title: Search in a Binary Search Tree

tuf.striver_title: Search in a Binary Search Tree

learnings.insight: The BST invariant means each comparison discards an entire subtree. Iteratively this is O(1) space, which is worth writing rather than defaulting to recursion out of habit.
learnings.trick: `while (r && r->val != key) r = key < r->val ? r->left : r->right;`. One line, no stack.
edge_cases: Returns null when absent, not a sentinel node.
The iterative form is genuinely O(1) space; the recursive form is O(h).
A degenerate tree makes this O(n).

complexity.why: each step eliminates one subtree. O(log n) when balanced, O(n) when degenerate.

followups.q: Why is O(h) not the same as O(log n)?
followups.a: Only a balanced tree has h = O(log n). Inserting sorted data gives a chain, and every BST operation degrades to linear.

followups.q: How does std::set avoid that?
followups.a: Red-black balancing - rotations and recolouring keep the longest path within twice the shortest.

problems.title: Insert into a Binary Search Tree

tuf.striver_title: Insert a given node in BST

learnings.insight: Descend to the null position the value belongs in and attach there. Any valid BST is an acceptable answer, so no rebalancing is required - which is exactly why repeated sorted insertion degenerates.
learnings.trick: Recurse and assign the result back: `r->left = insert(r->left, key)`. The null base case creates the node, and the assignment wires it in.
edge_cases: Empty tree returns a new single node.
Duplicates are excluded by constraint.
Assign the recursive result back, or the new node is created and discarded.

complexity.why: one descent to a leaf position.

followups.q: What happens if you insert sorted data?
followups.a: Every value goes to the same side and the tree becomes a linked list of height n. This is the motivation for self-balancing trees.

followups.q: Insert iteratively.
followups.a: Track a parent pointer while descending, then attach on the correct side. O(1) space.

learnings.insight: Three cases, and only the third is interesting. With zero or one child you splice. With two, you replace the value with the inorder successor - the smallest value in the right subtree - and then delete that successor, which by construction has at most one child.
learnings.trick: `if (!left) return right; if (!right) return left;` handles the easy cases. Then find the leftmost node of the right subtree, copy its value up, and recursively delete it.
edge_cases: The successor is the LEFTMOST node of the right subtree, not the right child.
Deleting the successor recursively is safe because it has at most one child.
Deleting the root must return the new root.
The predecessor works equally well - either is a valid answer.

complexity.why: one descent to find the node, plus one to find and remove the successor.

followups.q: Why the successor rather than any node?
followups.a: It is the smallest value greater than the deleted one, so placing it at the node preserves the BST invariant on both sides simultaneously.

followups.q: Why does the successor have at most one child?
followups.a: It is the leftmost node of a subtree, so by definition it has no left child.

problems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree

learnings.insight: In a BST the LCA is the first node whose value lies between the two targets - the point where their search paths diverge. No recursion and no subtree exploration is needed at all, which is a dramatic simplification over the general-tree version.
learnings.trick: Descend from the root. Both targets smaller means go left, both larger means go right, otherwise the current node is the answer.
edge_cases: A node may be its own ancestor - if p is an ancestor of q, p is the LCA and the split test handles it.
The targets may arrive in either order, so compare against both.
Iterative is O(1) space.

complexity.why: one descent. Compare with the general binary tree version, which must explore both subtrees at every node for O(n).

followups.q: Why is the BST version so much cheaper?
followups.a: The invariant tells you which side each target is on without looking. The general tree has no such information, so it must search both sides.

followups.q: What if a node might not be present?
followups.a: The split test still returns a node. Verify both targets exist with two searches, or the answer is meaningless.

problems.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST

tuf.striver_title: Kth Smallest and Largest element in BST

learnings.insight: Inorder on a BST yields sorted order, so the kth smallest is simply the kth element emitted. The follow-up about frequent modifications is where the real content is - and the answer is node augmentation.
learnings.trick: Iterative inorder with a counter, returning as soon as the count reaches k. Do not build the full sorted list.
edge_cases: Return early - building the whole list is O(n) when O(h + k) suffices.
k is 1-indexed.
A degenerate tree makes this O(n) regardless.

complexity.why: the descent to the smallest element is O(h), then k steps of the traversal. Collecting everything first is O(n).

followups.q: The tree is modified frequently and this query is common.
followups.a: Augment each node with its subtree size. Then descending is O(h) per query: at each node you know how many values lie to its left. This is an order-statistic tree.

followups.q: Why is augmentation the general answer?
followups.a: Any aggregate that can be computed from a node's children - size, sum, min, max - can be cached at the node and maintained in O(1) per structural change.

problems.title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree

learnings.insight: Choosing the middle element as root at every level is what produces balance. The sorted array is already an inorder traversal, so the only decision is where to split it - and the midpoint gives equal subtree sizes.
learnings.trick: Recurse on (lo, hi) taking mid as the root. Do not slice the array - pass indices, or you allocate O(n) at every level.
edge_cases: Passing sub-vectors instead of indices makes the space O(n log n).
Even-length ranges have two valid midpoints; either gives an accepted answer.
Empty range returns null.

complexity.why: each element becomes exactly one node, and the recursion is log n deep because the split is balanced.

followups.q: The input is a sorted linked list.
followups.a: LC 109. Either convert to an array first, or use the inorder-simulation trick: build left-to-right while advancing a list pointer, which is O(n) with no array.

followups.q: Why does taking the midpoint guarantee balance?
followups.a: It splits the remaining elements into two sets differing in size by at most one, at every level, which is exactly the balance condition.

learnings.insight: The point is the pruning, not the sum. When a node's value is below the range, its entire left subtree is irrelevant and can be skipped without examination - which is what makes this cheaper than a full traversal.
learnings.trick: If val < low, recurse right only. If val > high, recurse left only. Otherwise add and recurse both.
edge_cases: The range is inclusive on both ends.
Without pruning this is O(n) and the BST property is wasted.
Sums fit in int at these constraints, but check.

complexity.time: O(h + k) where k is the number of in-range nodes
complexity.why: pruned subtrees are never entered, so only the descent path plus the in-range region is visited.

followups.q: Why is the pruning correct?
followups.a: If a node's value is below low, every value in its left subtree is smaller still, so none can be in range. The invariant guarantees it without inspection.

followups.q: Trim the tree to the range instead.
followups.a: LC 669 - the same pruning, but rewiring rather than summing.

problems.title: Two Sum IV - Input is a BST

tuf.striver_title: Two Sum In BST | Check if there exists a pair with Sum K

learnings.insight: Three valid solutions with different trade-offs: a hash set during any traversal, an inorder array plus two pointers, or two BST iterators converging from both ends. The third is the O(h) space answer the follow-up wants.
learnings.trick: For the O(h) version, run a forward iterator from the smallest and a reverse iterator from the largest, moving whichever is needed - exactly two-pointer on a sorted array, without materialising it.
edge_cases: An element must not pair with itself - check that the two iterators have not met.
Duplicates are excluded by the BST property.
The hash-set solution is O(n) space and does not use the BST property at all.

complexity.space: O(h) with iterators, O(n) with a set
complexity.why: each node is visited once by one of the two iterators. The set version is simpler but ignores the sortedness entirely.

followups.q: Which solution would you give first?
followups.a: Name all three and their trade-offs. The set version is fastest to write; the dual-iterator version is what demonstrates you noticed it was a BST.

followups.q: Why does the set version not use the BST property?
followups.a: It would work identically on any binary tree. If a problem gives you a BST and your solution ignores that, expect a follow-up.

learnings.insight: The minimum difference in a BST is always between two values adjacent in sorted order, and inorder produces exactly that order. So one traversal comparing against the previous value suffices.
learnings.trick: Keep a `prev` pointer across the inorder traversal and take the minimum of `cur->val - prev`. Initialise prev to a sentinel or handle the first node.
edge_cases: prev must persist across recursive calls - a member variable or reference parameter.
At least two nodes are guaranteed.
Values are non-negative here, but the subtraction order still matters.

complexity.why: one traversal. Comparing all pairs is O(n^2) and ignores the BST property.

followups.q: Why must the minimum be between inorder-adjacent nodes?
followups.a: Sorted order places each value next to its nearest neighbours numerically. Any non-adjacent pair has something between them that is closer to both.

followups.q: LC 783 is the same problem.
followups.a: Identical, under a different name. Worth noticing how often that happens.

learnings.insight: Literally the same problem as LC 530 with a different title. Solving both back to back is a useful reminder to check whether a problem is one you have already done.
learnings.trick: Identical: inorder traversal tracking the previous value.
edge_cases: Same as LC 530 in every respect.
prev must survive across calls.
At least two nodes guaranteed.

complexity.why: one inorder pass.

followups.q: Why do duplicate problems exist on LeetCode?
followups.a: Different contributors, different years. The practical lesson is to search your own solved list before starting from scratch.

learnings.insight: Rewire the tree into a right-only chain in inorder order. Doing it during the traversal with a trailing pointer avoids building a list first, and it is the same shape as flattening a binary tree.
learnings.trick: Inorder traversal keeping a `tail` pointer. At each node, null its left, attach it to tail->right, and advance tail. A dummy head removes the first-node case.
edge_cases: Left pointers must be nulled, or the result is not a proper chain.
A dummy head avoids special-casing the first node.
Rewiring during traversal requires care not to lose the right subtree - visit it before reassigning.

complexity.why: one traversal rewiring two pointers per node.

followups.q: How does this relate to flattening a binary tree?
followups.a: Same operation in a different traversal order - preorder there, inorder here. Both use a trailing pointer and null one side.

learnings.insight: Materialising the whole inorder list is O(n) space and defeats the purpose. Keeping only the left spine on a stack gives O(h) space with amortised O(1) next() - the recursion's state made explicit and paused.
learnings.trick: Push the entire left spine in the constructor. next() pops, then pushes the left spine of the popped node's right child. hasNext() is simply a non-empty stack.
edge_cases: Only the LEFT spine is pushed, never whole subtrees.
After popping, descend the right child's left spine, not the right child alone.
next() is O(h) worst case but O(1) amortised across n calls.

complexity.why: each node is pushed and popped exactly once across all calls, so n calls cost O(n) total despite individual calls costing up to O(h).

followups.q: Justify the amortised bound.
followups.a: Every node enters the stack once and leaves once over the iterator's lifetime. Total work across n calls is O(n), so O(1) each on average.

followups.q: Add a prev() operation.
followups.a: Keep a second stack for the right spine, or record visited nodes. Genuinely harder - LC 1586.

followups.q: Why is O(h) space better than O(n) here?
followups.a: For a balanced tree that is log n versus n, and the iterator may be abandoned early, in which case the unbuilt portion was never paid for.

tuf.striver_title: Correct BST with two nodes swapped

learnings.insight: An inorder traversal of a valid BST is strictly increasing. Two swapped nodes create either one descent, when they are adjacent, or two. Recording the right elements of those descents identifies both culprits.
learnings.trick: Track prev during inorder. On the FIRST descent record both prev and cur; on any LATER descent record only cur. Then swap the two recorded values.
edge_cases: Adjacent swaps produce exactly one descent - the second node is cur of that same descent.
Non-adjacent swaps produce two descents; take the first's prev and the last's cur.
Swap VALUES, not nodes, unless the problem requires structural preservation.
Morris traversal gives the O(1) space follow-up.

complexity.why: one traversal detecting at most two anomalies.

followups.q: Do it in O(1) space.
followups.a: Morris traversal - thread each node's predecessor to it, detect descents during the threaded walk, and undo the threads. That is the stated follow-up.

followups.q: Why does an adjacent swap give only one descent?
followups.a: Swapping neighbours in sorted order creates a single inversion. Non-adjacent swaps break the order at two separate points.

learnings.insight: Each node must be increased by the sum of everything larger, so traverse in REVERSE inorder - right, node, left - accumulating as you go. The reversal is the entire insight.
learnings.trick: Keep a running sum. Recurse right, add the node's value to the sum, assign the sum back to the node, then recurse left.
edge_cases: The running sum must persist across calls - a member or reference parameter.
The node's new value is the sum AFTER adding its own value.
LC 1038 is the identical problem.

complexity.why: one traversal with constant work per node. Computing each node's greater-sum independently would be O(n^2).

followups.q: Why reverse inorder specifically?
followups.a: It visits values in descending order, so when you arrive at a node every larger value has already been accumulated.

followups.q: LC 1038 is the same problem.
followups.a: Identical. Another duplicate worth recognising rather than re-solving.

problems.title: Binary Search Tree to Greater Sum Tree

learnings.insight: The same problem as LC 538 under a different title. Worth solving only as a two-minute confirmation that the reverse-inorder accumulation is now automatic.
learnings.trick: Identical: reverse inorder with a running sum.
edge_cases: Same as LC 538.
Running sum persists across calls.
Assign after adding.

complexity.why: one reverse-inorder pass.

followups.q: How quickly did you recognise the duplicate?
followups.a: If it took more than ten seconds, the reverse-inorder pattern is not yet automatic. Redo LC 538 cold tomorrow.

learnings.insight: When a node is below the range, the node AND its entire left subtree are out, so the answer is whatever trimming its right subtree returns. Returning the recursive result directly is what makes this four lines rather than a case analysis.
learnings.trick: `if (val < low) return trim(right); if (val > high) return trim(left);` then recurse into both and return the node.
edge_cases: Return the recursive call's result directly when out of range - do not attempt to rewire.
The range is inclusive.
The root itself may be trimmed away.

complexity.time: O(n) worst, far less with pruning
complexity.why: each node is visited at most once, and entire subtrees are skipped when the invariant proves them out of range.

followups.q: Why can you discard the left subtree when val < low?
followups.a: Every value there is smaller than val, which is already below low. The invariant proves them all out of range without inspection.

followups.q: How does this differ from Binary Tree Pruning?
followups.a: Pruning has no ordering to exploit and must examine every node. Trimming can skip whole subtrees, which is the BST invariant paying off.

problems.title: Construct Binary Search Tree from Preorder Traversal

tuf.striver_title: Construct a BST from a preorder traversal

learnings.insight: Preorder alone is enough for a BST, because the invariant supplies the shape that a second traversal would otherwise provide. Carrying an upper bound down the recursion makes the construction linear rather than quadratic.
learnings.trick: Consume preorder with a shared index. Recurse with an upper bound; stop as soon as the next value exceeds it. Left gets the current node's value as its bound; right inherits the parent's.
edge_cases: Without the bound, splitting by scanning for the first larger element is O(n^2) on a degenerate tree.
The index must be shared by reference across all calls.
A strictly increasing preorder produces a right-leaning chain.

complexity.why: each value is consumed exactly once, with the bound test doing the splitting in O(1).

followups.q: Why does a BST need only one traversal?
followups.a: The ordering invariant determines which side each value belongs on, which is exactly the information inorder supplies for a general tree.

followups.q: Serialise a BST compactly.
followups.a: Preorder alone, no null sentinels - LC 449. That is this construction run in reverse.

followups.q: The same bound idea appears where else?
followups.a: Validating a BST. Construction and validation are the same range propagation, used to build versus to check.

learnings.insight: Choosing a root splits the remaining nodes into a left group and a right group whose counts multiply. Summing over every root choice gives the Catalan recurrence, and the whole problem is two nested loops.
learnings.trick: `dp[n] = sum over i of dp[i] * dp[n-1-i]`, with dp[0] = 1. The empty tree counting as one arrangement is what makes the base case work.
edge_cases: dp[0] = 1, not 0 - an empty subtree is one valid arrangement.
The values do not matter, only the count, because any n distinct values give the same structural count.
Catalan numbers grow fast but fit in int for n <= 19.

complexity.why: two nested loops over the DP table. The closed form C(2n,n)/(n+1) is O(n) but needs careful overflow handling.

followups.q: Derive the recurrence.
followups.a: With root i, the left subtree holds i nodes and the right holds n-1-i. Their counts are independent, so they multiply; summing over i gives the total.

followups.q: Where else do Catalan numbers appear?
followups.a: Balanced bracket sequences, triangulations of a polygon, and monotonic lattice paths - which is why Generate Parentheses has the same count.

learnings.insight: The counting version is DP; generating them all is necessarily exponential, because the output itself is Catalan-many trees. The structure is the same - choose a root, combine every left option with every right option.
learnings.trick: Recurse on a value range returning a vector of trees. For each root choice, take the Cartesian product of the left and right result lists.
edge_cases: An empty range must return a vector containing one nullptr, not an empty vector - otherwise the product is empty and whole branches vanish.
Subtrees can be shared between results, or deep-copied; sharing is accepted here.
n <= 8 by constraint, because the output explodes.

complexity.why: the output size is the Catalan number, and each tree costs O(n) to assemble.

followups.q: Why must the empty range return {nullptr}?
followups.a: The Cartesian product of an empty list with anything is empty, which would discard every tree having an empty subtree. A list containing one null keeps the product non-trivial.

followups.q: Memoise by range.
followups.a: Trees for range [i, j] depend only on its length when values are consecutive, so results can be reused with an offset.

problems.title: All Elements in Two Binary Search Trees

learnings.insight: Two inorder traversals produce two sorted lists, and merging them is the standard linear merge. The O(h) space follow-up runs two BST iterators in lockstep instead of materialising either list.
learnings.trick: Collect both inorders, then merge with two pointers. For O(h) space, use two stack-based iterators and advance whichever holds the smaller value.
edge_cases: Duplicates across the two trees are both kept.
Either tree may be empty.
Sorting the concatenation is O(n log n) and throws away the sortedness.

complexity.space: O(n + m), or O(h1 + h2) with iterators
complexity.why: two linear traversals plus a linear merge. Concatenating and sorting would be O(n log n).

followups.q: Do it in O(h1 + h2) space.
followups.a: Two BST iterators, advancing whichever front is smaller. This is the k-way merge idea with k = 2 and the lists never materialised.

followups.q: Why not concatenate and sort?
followups.a: It works and is one line, but it discards the fact that both inputs are already sorted - which is the whole reason the problem gives you BSTs.

learnings.insight: Rather than rotating, flatten the tree to a sorted array via inorder and rebuild it balanced from the midpoint. Two operations you already know, composed - which beats implementing AVL rotations under time pressure.
learnings.trick: Inorder into a vector, then run Convert Sorted Array to BST on it.
edge_cases: Any balanced arrangement is accepted, so the midpoint choice is free.
O(n) extra space for the array; the Day-Stout-Warren algorithm does it in O(1).
An already-balanced tree is rebuilt unnecessarily but correctly.

complexity.why: one traversal to flatten and one linear pass to rebuild.

followups.q: Do it in O(1) extra space.
followups.a: Day-Stout-Warren: rotate the tree into a right-leaning vine, then perform a series of left rotations to balance it. Worth naming; rarely worth implementing.

followups.q: Why is this easier than AVL rebalancing?
followups.a: AVL maintains balance incrementally on every insert. This rebuilds once, which is simpler when you do not need the invariant preserved between operations.

problems.title: Find Mode in Binary Search Tree

learnings.insight: Duplicates in a BST are adjacent in inorder order, so counting modes is a run-length scan rather than a frequency map. That is what satisfies the O(1) extra space follow-up.
learnings.trick: Inorder with a prev value and a run counter. Reset the run on a change; when the run beats the best, clear the result list and start over; when it ties, append.
edge_cases: Several modes may tie - the result is a list, not a single value.
The final run must be evaluated after the traversal ends.
A frequency map is O(n) space and is what the follow-up rules out.

complexity.space: O(h) for recursion, O(1) with Morris
complexity.why: one traversal with constant state. The map-based solution is simpler but ignores the sortedness.

followups.q: Why can you avoid a frequency map here?
followups.a: Equal values are contiguous in inorder, so a running count suffices. On an unordered tree you would need the map.

followups.q: The two-pass trick.
followups.a: One pass to find the maximum run length, a second to collect every value achieving it. Avoids clearing and rebuilding the result list.

problems.title: Count Nodes Equal to Average of Subtree

learnings.insight: Return a (sum, count) pair from each node so the parent can compute its own average in constant time. Computing each subtree's average independently would be O(n^2).
learnings.trick: Return {sum, count}. The average uses integer division, so compare `sum / count == node->val` exactly as specified.
edge_cases: Integer division truncates, which is the intended behaviour here.
A leaf always equals its own average and is always counted.
Null returns {0, 0}.

complexity.why: one traversal returning a small tuple, which is the general fix for 'each node needs an aggregate of its subtree'.

followups.q: Why return a pair rather than two traversals?
followups.a: Sum and count are both needed at every node. One traversal returning both is O(n); computing either separately per node is O(n^2).

followups.q: This does not use the BST property at all.
followups.a: Correct - it works on any binary tree. Worth noticing when a BST-tagged problem does not actually need the invariant.

problems.title: Number of Ways to Reorder Array to Get Same BST

learnings.insight: The root is fixed as the first element. Any interleaving of the left and right subtrees' insertion orders produces the same tree, so the count is a binomial coefficient times each subtree's own count - a clean recursive combinatorial argument.
learnings.trick: ways(seq) = C(n-1, leftSize) * ways(left) * ways(right). Precompute Pascal's triangle modulo 1e9+7, and subtract one at the very end to exclude the original ordering.
edge_cases: Subtract 1 only once, at the top level, not at every recursion.
Modular arithmetic throughout - the counts explode immediately.
The relative order within each subtree's subsequence must be preserved.

complexity.why: partitioning at each level is linear and the recursion is O(n) deep in the worst case, with the binomial table costing O(n^2) to build.

followups.q: Why a binomial coefficient?
followups.a: The left and right insertion sequences must each keep their internal order, but they may be interleaved freely. Choosing which positions go to the left subtree is C(n-1, leftSize).

followups.q: Why subtract one?
followups.a: The problem asks for REORDERINGS, which excludes the original sequence itself.
